name: Vitamin E / ferulic acid

lead: Ferulic acid is a plant antioxidant that is blended with vitamins C and E in skincare serums marketed for brightening and protection against photoaging.
Research cited for it is mostly laboratory and review literature on antioxidant activity. The sources reviewed contain no clinical trial of the vitamin E plus ferulic acid pairing for pigment.

paras: It scavenges free radicals, and is believed to interfere with tyrosine use in melanin synthesis. It also absorbs some UV light.
The sources reviewed do not detail adverse effects for topical use. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a regulated drug.

lead: Ferulic acid is a plant-derived hydroxycinnamic acid used in skincare as an antioxidant, commonly formulated alongside vitamin C and vitamin E in brightening and anti-aging serums. This entry covers the antioxidant combination in that context.[1][2]

Laboratory and review literature describes ferulic acid as a strong free-radical scavenger, and a 2018 review discussed its antioxidant properties and possible application in skin products.[3][4] Wikipedia notes its topical uses as a UV absorber, a photoaging treatment and a treatment for skin darkening, with a believed mechanism of competitively inhibiting tyrosine in melanin formation.[2]
The sources reviewed contain no clinical trial of a vitamin E and ferulic acid combination for pigmentation or brightening; the reference material is largely chemical and laboratory.
infobox: Cell walls of grasses, rice bran, flaxseed, corn hulls[2]
Vitamin C and vitamin E serums

paras: Ferulic acid is an amber crystalline solid with low water solubility and acts as a reducing agent through a resonance-stabilized phenoxy radical, according to Wikipedia. It is widespread in plant cell walls, often bound to carbohydrates, and is a major human metabolite of chlorogenic acids.[2]

Reviews attribute ferulic acid's activity to free-radical scavenging and related effects.[3][4][5][6] Early work characterized its antioxidant potential,[7] and a 2018 paper in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology discussed its possible application in skin products.[3] Wikipedia states that its darkening-reduction effect is believed to involve inhibition of tyrosine use in melanin synthesis.[2]

No studies found testing a vitamin E and ferulic acid combination for brightening or pigment in the sources reviewed. Registered trials of ferulic acid concern other uses, such as periodontitis adjunct therapy, bioavailability from bran and bread, and an antioxidant-capacity supplement in older adults.[8][9][10] One registered study examined topical agents with various antioxidant contents on photodamaged skin.[11]
Antioxidant serums combining ferulic acid with other vitamins are sold as cosmetics; a US drug-listing entry exists for one Spanish brand's topical ferulic acid, vitamin C and DMAE concentrate.[12]
